The carbon and oxygen in the carbonyl group, present in aldehydes and ketones are linked by a sigma bond and a pi bond. Both carbon as well as oxygen of the carbonyl group are sp²-hybridized. 19.2 Structure

Let us consider formaldehyde as an example to illustrate the structure of carbonyl group of aldehyde and ketone. The carbon and oxygen in the carbonyl group, present in aldehydes and ketones are linked by a sigma bond and a pi bond. Both carbon as well as oxygen of the carbonyl group are sp²-hybridized. The carbon-oxygen sigma and pi bonds are formed by linear sp²-sp² and sidewise overlap of p orbitals respectively. Two of the sp²-hybrid orbitals of oxygen has two unshared electron pairs, while two of the sp²-hybrid orbitals of carbon overlap with s orbitals of two hydrogen atoms to form carbon-hydrogen sigma bonds in formaldehyde (Figure 19.1).

Figure 19.1 Orbital hybridization model of formaldehyde.

The three atoms attached to carbonyl carbon lie in a plane and are arranged in trigonal planar manner. The carbon-oxygen bond length is 120 pm, which is significantly shorter than carbon-oxygen bond length in alcohols and ether (142 pm). The bond angles around carbonyl carbon are approximately 120°. Slight deviation is observed depending upon nature of atoms or groups attached to carbon in various aldehydes and ketones. The bond angles in some of the known aldehydes and ketones are shown in (Figure 19.2).

Figure 19.2 Bond angles in some aldehydes and ketones.

19.3 Physical Properties

Lower aldehydes like formaldehyde and acetaldehyde have very sharp pungent odour whereas higher members of aldehydes as well as most of the ketones have pleasant odour.

Formaldehyde is a gas at room temperature while other aldehydes are colourless volatile liquids. Formaldehyde is often stored and used as a 40% aqueous solution called formalin. Acetone and other members of ketone series are also colourless volatile liquids.

Aldehydes and ketones are polar compounds due to high dipole moment of their C=O bond. As a result they have higher boiling points than the corresponding alkanes and non-polar compounds like ethers. But they cannot form hydrogen bonds with themselves, therefore they usually have lower boiling points than corresponding alcohols. Boiling point of aldehydes and ketones increase with the increase in the molecular mass.

Lower aldehydes and ketones, upto four carbon atoms are water soluble. Water solubility decreases as the size of the non-polar alkyl group increases. Higher members of aldehydes and ketones are usually insoluble in water, while formaldehyde is highly soluble in water. Carbonyl compounds cannot form hydrogen bonds with themselves as there is no hydrogen on the carbonyl oxygen. However, their solubility in water is due to hydrogen bond formation of carbonyl oxygen with water molecules (Figure 19.3)

19.2 Structure

Let us consider formaldehyde as an example to illustrate the structure of carbonyl group of aldehyde and ketone. The carbon and oxygen in the carbonyl group, present in aldehydes and ketones are linked by a sigma bond and a pi bond. Both carbon as well as oxygen of the carbonyl group are sp²-hybridized. The carbon-oxygen sigma and pi bonds are formed by linear sp²-sp² and sidewise overlap of p orbitals respectively. Two of the sp²-hybrid orbitals of oxygen has two unshared electron pairs, while two of the sp²-hybrid orbitals of carbon overlap with s orbitals of two hydrogen atoms to form carbon-hydrogen sigma bonds in formaldehyde (Figure 19.1).

Figure 19.1 Orbital hybridization model of formaldehyde.

The three atoms attached to carbonyl carbon lie in a plane and are arranged in trigonal planar manner. The carbon-oxygen bond length is 120 pm, which is significantly shorter than carbon-oxygen bond length in alcohols and ether (142 pm). The bond angles around carbonyl carbon are approximately 120°. Slight deviation is observed depending upon nature of atoms or groups attached to carbon in various aldehydes and ketones. The bond angles in some of the known aldehydes and ketones are shown in (Figure 19.2).

Figure 19.2 Bond angles in some aldehydes and ketones.

19.3 Physical Properties

Lower aldehydes like formaldehyde and acetaldehyde have very sharp pungent odour whereas higher members of aldehydes as well as most of the ketones have pleasant odour.

Formaldehyde is a gas at room temperature while other aldehydes are colourless volatile liquids. Formaldehyde is often stored and used as a 40% aqueous solution called formalin. Acetone and other members of ketone series are also colourless volatile liquids.

Aldehydes and ketones are polar compounds due to high dipole moment of their C=O bond. As a result they have higher boiling points than the corresponding alkanes and non-polar compounds like ethers. But they cannot form hydrogen bonds with themselves, therefore they usually have lower boiling points than corresponding alcohols. Boiling point of aldehydes and ketones increase with the increase in the molecular mass.

Lower aldehydes and ketones, upto four carbon atoms are water soluble. Water solubility decreases as the size of the non-polar alkyl group increases. Higher members of aldehydes and ketones are usually insoluble in water, while formaldehyde is highly soluble in water. Carbonyl compounds cannot form hydrogen bonds with themselves as there is no hydrogen on the carbonyl oxygen. However, their solubility in water is due to hydrogen bond formation of carbonyl oxygen with water molecules (Figure 19.3)
